description:
A recipe for an ideal(our) team:

A full cup of engineering

2 tablespoons of creativity

1 handful of passion

A generous pinch of universal design

Mix it all together and you will get the perfect blend to build Earth’s Jukebox.
summary:
We built Earth Jukebox to turn NASA space photography, Earth climate maps, and time-lapse videos into a tactile musical instrument. Powered by Python, FluidSynth and a custom ESP32 controller with a rotary dial and push-buttons, the software sweeps a three-part scanning line across visuals to play live stereo chords on warm sounding instruments like the Kalimba and Harp. Automatically adapting to what is on screen, it maps cold blues to low notes and hot reds to high notes on climate maps while muting text legends and translates bright stars against silent dark space into calming pentatonic harmonies.

Earth Jukebox addresses the challenge by turning static or evolving scientific datasets into an intuitive, zero-latency musical instrument that users can scrub through at their own pace via touch and sound. By pairing physical touch with intuitive sound, it opens up complex satellite imagery and deep-space visuals to blind and visually impaired people, while giving classrooms and science museums a hands-on way to hear how our planet changes over time.
details:
What does it do. And how does it work?

Earth Jukebox turns NASA space photos and Earth climate maps into live music. Pick a photo or video from the gallery and a scanning line, split into three sections (Left, Middle, and Right), sweeps across the image, playing a 3-note chord in stereo. The program detects what kind of image you're looking at on its own.

Blue cold areas play low notes, red hot areas play high notes, and stronger colors play louder. Map legends and corner text get muted on their own, so they don't trigger false notes.

In star fields, dark empty space stays silent. Bright stars trigger notes based on how bright and dense they're. You can let the scan line play through the image automatically or turn a physical dial (rotary encoder) to move across the image, or move through video frames, to hear how Earth changes over time.

What benefits does it have?

Hands-On Exploration: Rather than passively listening to a fixed audio file, users physically control the scan line at their own pace using a hardware dial, buttons, or keyboard.

Pleasant, Relaxing Sound: All notes are locked to a harmonious pentatonic scale and played on soft acoustic instruments, starting with the Kalimba, alongside Nylon Guitar, Harp, Piano, and Ocarina, so the music always sounds pleasant rather than harsh.

Instant Response: Image data is pre-calculated and saved in a smart cache so there is zero delay when moving between lines, photos, or video frames.

What's this project meant to do?

Our main goal is to make NASA’s visual data accessible to everyone, including blind and visually impaired people, by letting them take in satellite maps and deep-space images through sound and touch. It is also built for classrooms, museums, and science exhibitions (featuring a full-screen, demo mode), so the public can hear climate patterns, temperature shifts, and cosmic structures.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Coding Language: Python 3.

Software & Libraries: Pillow (PIL) and NumPy for image analysis, Tkinter for the visual interface and media gallery, FluidSynth (with General MIDI SoundFonts) for real-time sound generation, and FFmpeg for splitting videos into frames.

Hardware & Operating System: An ESP32 with a rotary encoder and push-buttons, hooked up over USB, running Linux (Fedora and Debian).

How is your project creative?

We turned scientific data into something you can play like a musical instrument, a "jukebox" for Earth and space. Flip the scan line from horizontal to vertical and the stereo sound follows it from left to right. Or keep the line on one geographic location while spinning the dial through a video to hear seasons and temperatures change over time

What factors did your team consider?

Ear Comfort: Raw data can sound noisy and sharp. So we added a Low-Pass Filter to cut harsh high frequencies, smooth note transitions (Legato), and gentle acoustic instruments.

Zero Delay (Latency): We tuned the audio buffer to ~11 milliseconds and triggered sound before screen redraws. That way the instrument reacts instantly when you turn the dial.

Simplicity & Reliability: An on-screen legend explains the sounds. We also added signal filtering (debounce) so the hardware dial never skips, and optimized the code to run smoothly.
